selectedOriginals.inspection: Full 2006 west exterior inspected: two gallery storeys, nine window bays per face, alternating round-headed lower windows and rectangular windows, upper framed panels, nine small oculus dormers per face. Five main bridge arches with triangular cutwaters and round lookouts; separate near-house service opening. Main house has three principal bays, divided mullioned windows, elaborate dormers and tall stone chimneys.

Gallery windows and cutwaters corroborated.

additionalInspected.caption:
Château de Chenonceau spans the River Cher, near the small village of Chenonceaux. It is one of the most well-known châteaux of the Loire valley. The current château was built in 1514-1522 on the foundations of an old mill and was later extended to span the river. The bridge over the river was built between 1556-1559.
The original château was torched in 1412 by King Charles VII to punish owner Jean Marques for supporting the Duke of Bourgogne and the English.

The son built a new château and fortified mill on the site. He sold the castle to Thomas Bohier in 1513 who destroyed the castle, though its 15th-century keep was left standing. He then built an entirely new residence between 1514 and 1522, much of what we see today.
additionalInspected.inspection: Full 2014 north approach original inspected: broad round Marques Tower with corbelled upper floor, cone roof, attached tall stair turret with its own cone, tall chimney, divided dormer and open cupola. Main north entrance, balcony, three major dormers, corner turrets and chapel visible. Planters/trees/people omitted.

additionalInspected.caption:
A castle near the small village of Chenonceaux in the Indre-et-Loire department of France. It was built on the site of an old mill on the River Cher.
It was built between the 15th and 16th centurys.
Mary Queen of Scots may have lived here when she was married to Francis II of France (when he was King of France from 1559-60).

The spelling of the Chateau was changed from Chenonceaux to Chenonceau during the French Revolution to please the local villagers, also to distance it from going from a symbol of Royalty to a Republic.
additionalInspected.artist: Elliott Brown from Birmingham, United Kingdom
additionalInspected.inspection: Full 2009 terrace original inspected from château: raised stone retaining terrace, perimeter balustrade, bridge and round bridge-end lookouts. Separate gardens and service house in background excluded.

sources.inspection: Owner architectural overview read: two-storey house with corner turrets on former mill foundations; gallery crossing the Cher on five arches; detached Marques Tower.

Owner visitor guide text read: Marques Tower and former fortress terrace; gallery 60m long, 6m wide, 18 windows total. These are interior room dimensions, not an exterior survey. Kitchens occupy the two enormous old mill bases; distinct connecting bridge/boat platform beneath house. Modern ground-floor plan and terrace illustration inspected separately during preparation.

Official API documentation read: resource selection, up to5000 points/request, five requests/second limit,2-decimal rounding and variable source accuracy. Used six sequential4500-point-or-smaller requests and preserved exact requests/responses. No effective native resolution claimed.
IGN primary open-data policy read: near-complete public geographic data distributed under Etalab2.0. Source attribution retained.

scope: Main château, river-spanning gallery with piers/arches and detached Marques tower as a coordinated immediate site.
limitations: Seven local originals individually inspected and all 61 candidate contacts reviewed. Many other candidates are interiors, other Loire châteaux, historical illustrations or an unbuilt grand proposal; they do not control current exterior geometry.

Main house, river gallery/five principal arches, mill foundation/boat arch, chapel, detached Marques Tower, immediate raised terrace and short approach bridge only. Gardens, Chancellerie, orangery, separate south service annex, landscape, people, interiors, heraldic inscriptions and photo textures excluded.

Native generalized map part heights are massing hints, not surveys. Owner gallery dimensions are internal. Fine carving, unobserved details, roof engineering, thresholds and vertical levels are conservative photo-based estimates.

Terrain acquisition precedes geometry. Original source pixels and sampled relief must remain unchanged. River DEM is a composite water/terrain surface and supplies no reliable bathymetry or current water level; no surveyed riverbed compatibility is claimed.

Gallery five principal arches and separate mill/entry bridge openings must remain actual voids in all four LODs. Nine gallery windows and nine oculus dormers per long face derive from the photographs and the owner’s 18-window total.

Original baseline Terrarium elevation is rejected for site QA; unchanged official IGN response values resolve the raised terrace and river. Future hosts with the rejected coarse field may bury bridge arches. This model is a bounded preview with footprint replacement disabled.
